paras: The lynching of George W. and Jim Fraley was the hanging of two brothers by an armed mob near Hazel Dell, Comanche County, Texas, in late 1882, after they had been arrested on a charge of stealing cotton. The mob took the brothers from their guard at night and hanged them from the same limb of a tree. Wire dispatches from Dallas carried the story to papers across the country, several of which stressed that the younger brother was 'a mere boy.'

According to the fuller Dallas dispatch, a constable arrested G. W. and Jim Fraley on warrants charging them with stealing cotton, and Jim was 'only nineteen years old.' The prisoners were taken to Hazel Dell and placed under guard. No paper gave the race of the brothers or of the men who killed them.

The two Dallas versions differ on how the mob got the prisoners. In the shorter wire, a mob armed with shotguns overpowered the guards at midnight, took the brothers to the woods and hanged them on the same limb. The fuller account said that about 10 o'clock at night 'a dozen men, armed with shotguns, induced the guard to give up the prisoners' and carried them about a mile. The next morning both were found dead, suspended from the same limb of a tree.

No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution of the mob appears in the coverage. The local Comanche Chief reportedly wrote that a double hanging 'by Judge Lynch' in the county had caused only 'a ripple' of excitement.

Within Texas the case drew comment before the wire reports spread: the Dallas Daily Herald of December 9 reprinted a Waco Examiner paragraph headed 'WHAT CONSTITUTES A RIPPLE', which mocked the Chief's phrase and noted that 'the poor devils who were hung had been charged—not convicted—of stealing cotton.' The Examiner suggested sarcastically that a country where such events caused only a ripple was a desirable place for 'nervous people, who value human life' to move to.

Outside Texas the story ran from December 19 as a brief Dallas dispatch, under headlines such as 'Two Brothers Lynched' in the St. Paul Daily Globe, 'Two Lads Lynched', 'Boy Brothers Lynched' in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and 'Hanged for Stealing Cotton'. Papers in Georgia, Kentucky and West Virginia printed it the same week, and the fuller version reached the Stark County Democrat in Ohio under the heading 'LYNCHING AT HAZEL DELL, TEXAS.' Weeklies folded it into news digests and crime columns, one saying the brothers 'were swung up to the limb of a tree', and a year-end chronology listed 'Two cotton thieves lynched at Hazel Dell' under December 18. None of these reprints added comment beyond the headline.

The date of the lynching is uncertain: the Dallas dispatches of December 18 reported the news as 'just received', while the Waco paragraph printed by December 9 placed a Comanche County double lynching of men charged with stealing cotton in the previous week. The Waco paragraph names no victims, so its link to the Fraleys rests on the place and the charge.
